name: James Russo
bio: Engineering lead for HyperFrames. Currently at HeyGen building the future of video storytelling, Previously at Brex

talks.title: HTML is All You Need (for Agents to Make Graphics)

quotes.quote: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the native languages of LLMs. Most of their training data, every webpage that gets scraped at the end of day is essentially just HTML, CSS, and JavaScript under the hood.
Uh we like to think of this as trying to ask Shakespeare to write a poem in Japanese or Chinese.
Um then we have HTML, which around November of last year when Gemini 3 and the latest models came out, we saw a step function improvement in what LLMs could do.
We played around with Remotion quite a bit and honestly thought it was a great example of what LLMs and agents could do with coding. Um however, we noticed that we had to teach them the framework.
Um and we decided, let's not fight the model, but find a way where we can let them talk in their native tongue.

So, how we did this was starting with a very small model, Gemini 3 Flash, as our design partner. We knew that if the smaller models could author workable code in a framework, then the larger models and these coding agents could 100% do it as well.
but to our surprise, the thinnest wrapper ultimately won, which is essentially just HTML at the end of the day with a few data attributes as metadata
The same pixels that the browser sees is ultimately what your video is going to see.
And this was a lot harder because browsers are async on purpose. Um they have a different set of requirements and concerns to video rendering.

We freeze the clock in the browser and then we seek deterministically to every single moment in time or every single frame, uh wait for everything to load on the page, ensure that it's loaded and ready to go, and then we take a screenshot and move on to the next frame
Things like 3.js, charts, SVGs, shaders, WebGL, WebGPU, Lottie, all of these are renderable in the browser, and therefore all of them are renderable in hyperframes.

Our skill is focused on taste and video aspects because the LLMs and agents already know how to write HTML and CSS and JavaScript, we don't have to teach them the language, we just teach them how to create good videos.

However, great output takes craft. Similar to AI coding, you can get decent output by just giving a single prompt and having something that works for your needs, but getting great output from agents requires craft, taste
Over 1.3 million videos have been rendered by open-source users of Hyperframes in the last 90 days. 267,000 creators have tried it.
We have about 15,000 videos every single day being rendered utilizing the open-source framework and 32,000 GitHub stars.
If your agent knows how to write HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, it knows how to create a Hyperframes video.
The one honest thing that we're going to say here is that the models still aren't good at creative work.

which is why we started to work on a code to video benchmark where we are trying to work with the LLM labs, any creators who are working on video agents to ensure that we can raise the floor of videos for everyone
agents are made building incredibly easy. Launching is still quite hard.
Most people think coding agents only write code. But if you ask me, that's just bad marketing.
You have to be able to think like an agent to get it to do what you want it to do.
Every day, the world pours something like 34,000 human years into making slide decks. Most of that time isn't the thinking, it's the fiddling.
A deck that takes 10 hours should really take about 25 minutes once you remove all the formatting and the branding and the moving things around.
Every one of these tools is built for human hands and human eyes.
There is a data structure underneath, but it's in a format that only the application can read.
AI skeptics say that it's not just the tools. Agents fundamentally can't reason about space.
If you ask me, it's not the model, it's the medium.
If I asked you, someone who is presumably human, to handwrite an SVG of a pelican, you wouldn't be able to do that either.
Asking an AI to use a canvas is like asking a human to write SVG by hand. It doesn't really make sense.
You need to give the AI tools based on how it thinks, not in pixels, in language. Words, tokens, structure, that is its native medium.
HTML lets the model think in structure. HTML tags have meanings built into the language.
So, the model never actually places a coordinate, and you can get all sorts of visual effects, charts and layouts, fonts and motion, all of it for free.
PowerPoint is a tool that you use to make slide decks. The deck itself, that's just the presentation mode.
The editing format is totally arbitrary.
What you're watching is just HTML and CSS. It's literally just divs all the way down.
Plain text is a choice, generally a choice of convenience, but it's usually the wrong one if you're actually trying to create something of use.
I do want to take a quick beat here and point out that a beautiful deck on its own is generally not worth anything.
Let your agents do all the grunt work while you focus on vision and story.
Stop thinking like a user. Think like the model. Give it the right language, and for graphics, all you need is HTML.

positions.claim: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the native languages of LLMs because most training data reduces to them, so agents produce better output in those languages than in a custom DSL or JSON schema.
Teaching a model a new DSL or custom JSON structure degrades output quality even when given many examples.
After Effects and Premiere Pro produce gold-standard creative output but are not agent-friendly; their connectors act as copilots rather than sources of creative output.
Lottie and Rive give decent output but are not agent-friendly and are less editable and controllable than HTML.
Remotion requires teaching agents the framework and its conventions, which reduces the creativity of the resulting output.
Around November of the prior year, with Gemini 3 and contemporaneous models, there was a step-function improvement in what LLMs could produce, and unprompted they gravitated toward HTML/CSS/JS.
The thinnest wrapper around HTML outperformed heavier alternatives with larger system prompts, more context, and added skills.
If a small model can author workable code in a format, larger coding agents certainly can, and the format will keep improving as models improve and training data accumulates.
Browsers are asynchronous by design, which makes them unsuitable for video rendering without freezing the clock and forcing full asset load per frame.
Anything renderable in a browser — Three.js, charts, SVGs, shaders, WebGL, WebGPU, Lottie — can be rendered into a Hyperframes video.
Agent skills should teach taste and domain craft rather than framework syntax, since the model already knows the underlying language.
Single-shot prompting yields decent video, but great video requires the same craft and iterative decomposition as pre-AI software engineering.
Hyperframes has rendered over 1.3 million videos for open-source users in 90 days, been tried by 267,000 creators, renders ~15,000 videos per day, and has 32,000 GitHub stars.
Current models are still not good at creative work, and improving this requires a shared code-to-video benchmark rather than better prompts alone.
Coding agents have made building easy, but launching a product — the post, the video — remains the harder bottleneck.
Humans should remain in the loop with a full manual editing surface, so power users can do anything they would do in a conventional video editor.
Agents' failure at graphics is caused by the medium they are given, not by a model limitation in spatial reasoning.
Coding agents are general-purpose agents; calling them 'coding' agents is a marketing artifact that understates what they can do.
The pelican-in-SVG test measures the difficulty of the medium more than the model's spatial ability, since humans also cannot hand-write such an SVG.
Canvas-based agent tooling — Figma MCPs, PowerPoint CLIs, screenshot-and-replace loops — is the wrong approach because it makes agents imitate human interaction patterns.
HTML is the right authoring medium for agent-generated graphics because models have trained on billions of examples of it and its tags carry layout semantics.
The editing format of a deck does not matter because audiences only ever see the presentation mode, so you can choose HTML and render to PDF later.
Roughly 34,000 human years per day go into making slide decks, most of it formatting rather than thinking.
A 10-hour deck should take about 25 minutes if formatting, branding, and layout fiddling were removed.
Plain text is usually the wrong output default for agents producing artifacts meant to be used.
Formatting is the easy half of the problem; the real value comes from connecting the model to company data so it can source deck content itself.
Arc AGI-style benchmarks are built on the premise that agents cannot reason about space, a premise the speaker rejects.
